wine.name: Brunello di Montalcino Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva of the Brunello di Montalcino DOCG, released from the sixth year after the harvest
wine.grapes: Sangiovese alone, the strain the estate calls Sangiovese Grosso, from its own vines at Greppo.
wine.sites: The Greppo hillside south east of Montalcino town, between about 300 and 500 metres by an estate sheet, on stony soils of mixed origin, the galestro shale prized among them; the Riserva comes from the oldest vines, over twenty five years old.
wine.making: By the estate's sheet for the 2016 vintage, the grapes ferment with native yeasts in upright Slavonian oak vats. The wine then ages for three years in large Slavonian oak casks, with no new wood, and rests in bottle until its release, no sooner than 1 January of the sixth year after the harvest. A Riserva is made only in years the estate judges worthy.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, dried rose and tea leaf over iron and a touch of leather; pale garnet, taut and high toned, with high acidity, fine but firm tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Closed and severe for its first decade or more, it unfolds over many decades; the estate keeps bottles of its 1888 and 1891 Riservas in its own cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle two hours ahead, and stand an old one upright for a day before pouring it off its sediment; a large, tulip shaped glass.

records.table: Biondi-Santi's Brunello di Montalcino Riserva comes from Greppo, where Ferruccio Biondi Santi made the 1888 the consorzio counts as the first wine labelled Brunello di Montalcino. Sangiovese alone, aged three years in large Slavonian casks, it is pale, taut and slow to open, so decant it and give it time.
records.story: Greppo belonged to the Santi family in the nineteenth century, and by the consorzio's account the first wine to win recognition under the name Brunello, of the 1865 vintage, was made by a Montalcino chemist of that family and honoured in 1869. His grandson Ferruccio Biondi Santi, who died in 1917, held to Sangiovese alone and to long ageing in large casks while oidium and phylloxera threatened the region's vines. His 1888 is counted by the consorzio as the first wine officially labelled Brunello di Montalcino, and bottles of it are kept at Greppo, topped up and recorked in 1927, 1970 and 1985. Ferruccio's son and then his grandson carried the estate through the twentieth century. Brunello became a DOC in 1966 and, by the consorzio's account, Italy's first DOCG in 1980, and the estate's own Sangiovese selection was registered as the clone BBS11 in 1978. The grandson died in 2013, and at the end of 2016 the family sold a majority of the estate to the French group EPI. The Riserva is where the denomination's long ageing began: when a guest asks what Brunello was before it was a rule, this is the bottle to explain it.

The estate's English page calls Ferruccio the nephew of Clemente Santi, a reading of the Italian nipote; the consorzio and Italian Wikipedia say grandson, the son of Caterina Santi, and the record follows them.

Clemente Santi is described, not named: only Italian Wikipedia gives his dates (1795 to 1885); Ferruccio's death in 1917 rests on the importer Wilson Daniels and two trade profiles, and no source read gave his birth year, so he carries his death alone.
Ferruccio's son is not named because people.json lists Tancredi Biondi Santi, a living descendant who shares the name of the grandfather (died 1970).
The sale to EPI rests on Wine Spectator (completed 16 December 2016), Decanter and WineNews; one Decanter piece says 2017, so the story says the end of 2016.

The consorzio's page for the estate says the Riserva is now chosen by soil and exposure rather than vine age, and the 2013 sheet says only the oldest parcels; the library's Riserva means older vines here may need a softer word.
The altitude of Greppo is given as about 450 to 560 metres in different trade profiles; the record says around 500 metres. Search count for this record: 9 of the group's 35.

wine.name: Brunello di Montalcino
wine.classification: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, granted to Brunello di Montalcino in 1980
wine.grapes: Sangiovese only, picked by hand from the oldest vines on the estate.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards around Sant'Angelo in Colle, some ten kilometres south of Montalcino, between 150 and 450 metres, in a warm, breezy corner between Monte Amiata and the sea; its Sangiovese is selected from the estate's own old vines.
wine.making: Fermented for fifteen to twenty days in stainless steel with native yeasts, the cap of skins kept submerged in the wine throughout; malolactic follows in steel. The wine then ages for about three years in large French oak casks of 30 and 50 hectolitres before resting in bottle.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry and plum with tobacco leaf, dried rose and a touch of liquorice; generous and warm for Brunello, with fresh acidity and firm, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Drinks from about eight to ten years after the vintage and keeps for twenty years and more in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter suits a young bottle, while an older one wants a slow pour off its deposit; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Il Poggione's Brunello di Montalcino comes from Sant'Angelo in Colle, in the warm south of the hill: Sangiovese from the estate's oldest vines, fermented with the cap kept under the wine and aged about three years in large French casks. Ripe and generous, it shows the southern face of Brunello.
records.story: Late in the nineteenth century, as the family tells it, a Florentine landowner heard a shepherd who wintered his flock around Montalcino describe the country around Sant'Angelo in Colle; he went to see it, bought land there and founded the farm his descendants have kept ever since. The estate counts itself among the first to sell its wine as Brunello di Montalcino, early in the twentieth century. In 1964 the family planted Vigna Paganelli on an alluvial terrace, the vineyard that gives its Riserva. Brunello was made a DOC in 1966, and in 1967, when the growers formed the consorzio, the house was, by its own account, among its founding members; the DOCG followed in 1980. Through those decades the Brunello kept a method of its own. The grapes ferment in stainless steel with the cap of skins held under the wine, and the wine spends about three years in large casks of French oak before it is bottled. Its warmth is the warmth of the south of the hill, between Monte Amiata and the sea air. Taught beside Biondi-Santi's Greppo, higher on the hill and nearer the town, Il Poggione shows how the south of Montalcino gives a riper, rounder Sangiovese.

wine.name: Poggio all'Oro Brunello di Montalcino Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva under the Brunello di Montalcino DOCG, released from the sixth year after the harvest
wine.grapes: Sangiovese alone, as every Brunello must be.
wine.sites: A single vineyard on a broad plateau at about 230 to 250 metres, on brown clay and silt holding calcareous stones and pebbles that drain well.
wine.making: Made only in years the estate judges worthy. Since the estate built its Horizon tanks, which join French oak to stainless steel, it has fermented in them at controlled temperature; earlier vintages fermented in steel. From 2015 it has spent thirty months or more in French oak, most of it in casks of 60 to 90 hectolitres and the rest in 350 litre barrels.
wine.glass: Red cherry and black plum with iris, cigar box and a touch of vanilla; fuller and rounder than the Greppo style, with lively acidity and polished, supple tannin.
wine.ageing: Released no sooner than the sixth year after the harvest, it opens over the next few years and holds for twenty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the estate suggests; decant for an hour to lift the perfume and pour a mature bottle off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Poggio all'Oro is Castello Banfi's single vineyard Brunello di Montalcino Riserva, first made in 1985 from one broad plateau, and only in chosen years. Riper and rounder than the old school, with polished tannin, it shows the modern Montalcino a New York family built.
records.story: The name is older than the estate. The import firm the Mariani family founded in New York in 1919 was named, as the family tells it, for a woman who was the first lay person to run a pope's household. From 1969 its fortune grew on Riunite Lambrusco, which it sold across the United States. In 1978 two brothers of the second generation came to Montalcino and founded Castello Banfi on land in the south west of the zone. Studies of the estate's soils began in 1980, mapping where Sangiovese would do well; in 1983, by the estate's own timeline, it acquired the medieval castle of Poggio alle Mura, and the winery opened on 12 September 1984. The first Poggio all'Oro followed with the 1985 vintage, a Riserva from one plateau, made only in years the estate judges worthy. Banfi brought scale, a technical cellar and an American sales network to a small hill town, and the estate credits one of the brothers with launching Brunello in the United States. For a sommelier the Riserva answers a fair question: whether a large estate can bottle a single site with the patience Brunello asks.

wine.name: Brunello di Montalcino Tenuta Nuova
wine.classification: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita; Tenuta Nuova is a vineyard name, not an official cru
wine.grapes: Sangiovese, and nothing else, from the estate's own vines on the Tenuta Nuova site.
wine.sites: Tenuta Nuova, the new property, is land where, by the estate's account, nobody had planted Sangiovese before, chosen after a study of the local microclimates and their exposures, with its clones, rootstocks and planting density chosen by study as well.
wine.making: Bunches are picked by hand and passed through an optical sorter, then ferment with native yeasts for about twenty four days in truncated cone stainless steel tanks at controlled temperature. The wine then spends some thirty months or more in oak, by the 2019 vintage in French tonneaux in place of barriques, and a year or more in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry and plum with espresso, cocoa and a touch of clove; darker, rounder and more polished than the traditional camp, with ripe, firm tannin and fresh acidity under the fruit.
wine.ageing: Approachable sooner than traditional Brunello, it opens from about eight years after the vintage and holds for fifteen to twenty years in a strong year.
wine.serve: Pour at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius after an hour or two in a decanter; a large glass with a wide bowl.

label.means: New property: the name the house gave a site it planted to Sangiovese for the first time.

records.table: Tenuta Nuova is Casanova di Neri's Brunello di Montalcino from land that, as the estate tells it, had never carried Sangiovese, first made in 1993. Dark, polished and generous, it is the modern style of Montalcino in a glass.
records.story: In 1971 the founder began to farm on the eastern side of Montalcino, and the estate dates its first Brunello harvest to 1978. Its first vineyard, as the estate tells it, was Cerretalto, a natural amphitheatre above the Asso river, followed in time by Le Cetine, Pietradonice and Podernovo. In 1991 the founder handed the estate to his son, and two years later came the wine that changed its standing: Tenuta Nuova, the new property, first made in 1993 from land where, as the estate tells it, nobody had grown Sangiovese, chosen after a study of the local microclimates. Riper, darker and more polished than the Brunello of the old houses, it carried the modern style of Montalcino to a wide audience. Cerretalto, bottled on its own from the 1981 vintage, appears only in selected years. By the 2019 vintage the house had moved towards shorter maceration and gentler oak, ageing Tenuta Nuova in French tonneaux rather than barriques. Montalcino has no official cru system, so the name on the label is the estate's own. Set beside Biondi-Santi or Soldera, Tenuta Nuova is the other side of the old argument in Montalcino between large old casks and smaller, newer wood.

wine.name: Soldera Case Basse Sangiovese
wine.appellation: Toscana IGT, written Toscana IGP on later labels
wine.grapes: Sangiovese alone, from the estate's own vines, picked by hand.
wine.sites: The Case Basse and Intistieti vineyards near Tavernelle in the south west of Montalcino, at about 320 metres, farmed beside a botanical garden of roses, with nesting boxes and beehives among the rows for the birds and insects that keep the vines healthy.
wine.making: The berries are checked one by one, then ferment spontaneously with native yeasts in large Slavonian oak vats. The wine then ages for several years in large Slavonian oak casks before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Pale garnet; dried rose, sour cherry and orange peel over forest floor and a note of tea, light in colour and weight yet long and searching, with silky tannin and bright acidity.
wine.ageing: Released only after long cask ageing, it drinks from about ten years after the vintage and develops for decades in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant gently an hour ahead, pouring an older bottle slowly off its sediment; a large Burgundy glass for the perfume.

label.means: The regional category the estate has used since the 2006 vintage in place of Brunello, written IGP on later labels.
The farm near Tavernelle bought in 1972, its name printed beside Soldera's.
The one grape, which a Toscana wine may name on its label.

records.table: Soldera Case Basse is pure Sangiovese from a Montalcino estate founded in 1972, fermented with native yeasts in large oak vats and aged for years in big Slavonian casks. Since the 2006 vintage it has carried Toscana IGT, not Brunello, on its label.
records.story: Gianfranco Soldera (1937 to 2019), born in Treviso, was an insurance broker in Milan when, in 1972, he and his wife went looking for a wine estate and bought Case Basse, a farm near Tavernelle in the south west of Montalcino. Together they planted it afresh and set a botanical garden of roses beside the vines, with nests and hives for the birds and insects that keep the vines healthy. In the cellar he fermented with native yeasts in large oak vats and aged his wine for years in big Slavonian casks; in good years it was bottled as Brunello di Montalcino Riserva. On the night of 2 December 2012 a former employee opened the taps of his casks, and most of the wine of six vintages, 2007 to 2012, ran to waste. Fellow producers and the consorzio offered wine of their own to make good the loss, and he turned it down; in March 2013 he left the consorzio. From the 2006 vintage, which the attack did not reach, his wine has been labelled Toscana IGT. He died in February 2019. Case Basse shows that a Montalcino Sangiovese can be famous with no Brunello on its label.

others.name: Brunello di Montalcino Riserva Case Basse
others.note: The label of good vintages before 2006; other years were bottled as Brunello di Montalcino.

traps: From the 2006 vintage Soldera is Toscana IGT, not Brunello di Montalcino, though it is pure Sangiovese grown inside the Brunello zone.
The vandalism of December 2012 destroyed most of the 2007 to 2012 wine in cask, which is why certain years are missing or scarce.
Intistieti is one of the estate's two vineyard plots, beside Case Basse, not a separate producer.

cards.front: Soldera Case Basse: why does the label say Toscana IGT rather than Brunello di Montalcino?
cards.back: The estate left the Brunello consorzio in 2013, after the vandalism of 2012, and chose Toscana IGT from the 2006 vintage, trusting its own name over Brunello's.

cards.front: What happened in the Case Basse cellar of Soldera on the night of 2 December 2012?
cards.back: A former employee opened the taps of the casks, and most of the wine of the 2007 to 2012 vintages was lost.

questions.q: A guest asks how Soldera ferments Case Basse. Which answer fits?
opts: Native yeasts in large Slavonian oak vats
Cultured yeasts in temperature controlled steel
Carbonic maceration in sealed concrete tanks
Whole clusters in clay amphorae
questions.exp: The estate ferments spontaneously with native yeasts in large Slavonian oak vats; it uses no cultured yeasts, and its vats are oak, not steel.

questions.q: Before he bought Case Basse in 1972, what was Gianfranco Soldera's trade?
opts: An insurance broker in Milan
A chemist in Montalcino
A wine importer in New York
A cooper in Slavonia
questions.exp: He was an insurance broker in Milan; the chemist is in the Santi story at Greppo, and the New York importers founded Banfi.

report: Label before and after 2012, as the plan asks: Brunello di Montalcino, a Riserva in good years, through the 2005 vintage; from the 2006 vintage, bottled before the attack and released after he left the consorzio, Toscana IGT, written Toscana IGP from 2013, by the estate's own list of wines.

The founder's dates: born 1937 in Treviso by Wikipedia and a critic's obituary that cannot be cited here; died 16 February 2019 at 82 by Wine Spectator and Decanter. His widow and children are living and are not named, nor is the former employee jailed for the attack.

The loss is given as about 62,600 litres by Decanter and more than 16,500 gallons by Wine Spectator, with Wine-Searcher later reporting that about a quarter survived, so the record says most of the wine of six vintages.
The estate's own list shows releases headed 2007 to 2008 and 2011 to 2012, which may be wines of two vintages bottled together; that was not confirmed and is left out.
The library places the botanical garden between the rows; Wikipedia gives a botanical park beside the vineyards, so the record says beside the vines.
Up to six years in cask rests on Wikipedia and a writer's profile that cannot be cited; the first vintage of 1975 and the first Brunello of 1977 rest on that obituary alone and are left out.
Decanter's report of the resignation adds that the consorzio expelled him at once; that rests on one source and is left out.
Search count for this record: 6 of the group's 35, one of them refused for a blocked domain.

changed: wine.making and questions: was truncated cone vats of more than 100 hectolitres with no temperature control, up to six years in cask and no filtration; now large Slavonian oak vats after the berries are checked one by one, and several years in large casks, since the estate gives vats of over 100 quintals, its 2019 sheet says the fermentation temperature is continuously monitored, and the six years and the filtration rested on one citable source.
wine.appellation and wine.label: was IGP from the 2013 vintage; now IGP on later labels, since the estate's 2019 and 2021 sheets are headed Toscana IGP but the year of the change was not confirmed.

wine.sites and story: the creatures that prey on vine pests are now the birds and insects that keep the vines healthy, with the nests and hives among the rows, as the estate's natural vinegrowing page gives it.
story: the founder's quoted reason for refusing the offered wine cut, on no source read; producers and the consorzio offered wine and he turned it down, as the drinks press gives it.
story: resigned is now left, since English reports speak of a resignation and Italian ones of an expulsion.

story and others: in good years the whole crop became Riserva is now in good years it was bottled as Riserva; a run down farm is now a farm; the 2006 already in bottle is now which the attack did not reach, since the casks held 2007 to 2012.
others and traps: the Intistieti label of 1985 to 1992 cut, on no source read; Intistieti is now one of the estate's two vineyard plots, as the estate gives it.
cards: the reason for Toscana IGT is now the estate's own, a choice to trust its own name over Brunello's, by the estate and the founder's words in the trade press.
questions: a pharmacist in Montalcino is now a chemist, matching the Biondi-Santi record.
open: The night of the attack is 2 December by Wikipedia and the night of 2 to 3 December by the family's statement; the record says the night of 2 December.
